title: Countless favors
hookLine: if you counted Allah's favors you could not number them (16:18)

cards: Surah sixteen is called an-Nahl, the Bee, after a few verses near its middle. But some early scholars gave it another name: the surah of favors. The opening reads like an inventory.

Cattle, for warmth, for food, and, the verse adds, for beauty, when you bring them home in the evening and drive them out in the morning. Horses and mules to ride, and as an adornment. Rain to drink, and for the pastures.
Stars to steer by at night. The sea, with fresh fish and things to wear. Then, after the list, the surah stops counting.

teach.b: Verse eighteen, in Pickthall's translation: "And if ye would count the favour of Allah ye cannot reckon it. Lo! Allah is indeed Forgiving, Merciful." The word is ni'mah, a favor, a blessing, a grace.
Some commentators point out it's singular. If you tried to count the favor of God, not the favors, you couldn't. Take one: your breath.
It depends on lungs, on air, on a planet with the right mix of gases, on the night you slept through without thinking about it once. One favor opens into a thousand.
There's an almost identical verse in Surah Ibrahim, from last week, verse thirty-four. Same opening: if you counted God's favor, you couldn't number it.
But it ends differently: truly, man is unjust, ungrateful. Here, in an-Nahl, it ends: truly, God is forgiving, merciful. Commentators have long noticed the pair.
One verse looks at what people do with the favors: forget them, waste them, take them as owed.

The other looks at what God does in return: forgives, and keeps giving anyway. You can't count the favors, or the times they went unthanked, and both verses say so. The surah's list isn't meant to be finished.

You start counting cattle and rain, and somewhere around the stars, you realize the counting is hopeless. That moment, when the list fails, is the point. Last week: if you give thanks, I will give you more.
Today: you couldn't count them if you tried.

how: Muslims recite 16:18 and 14:34 as reminders of God's favors, and many teachers have students list blessings to see the list break down, answering with alhamdulillah.

o: a reward earned by doing good deeds
a debt of thanks that must be repaid
a favor, a blessing, a grace from God

games.q: the surah of favors — tap the pairs.
p: a favor, a blessing, a grace
the Bee, also called the surah of favors

s: 16:18 speaks of God's favor in the singular
commentators note it: even one favor of God can't be counted.
the verses in 14:34 and 16:18 end the same way
one ends with human ingratitude, the other with God's forgiveness and mercy.
an-Nahl's list of favors includes beauty
cattle bring beauty when driven home in the evening and out in the morning.

games.q: you sit down to count every favor God has given you, one by one. what does 16:18 say happens?
o: you won't be able to number them.
games.why: if you would count the favor of God, you cannot reckon it; and God is forgiving, merciful.

practice: Start counting favors, one per breath: your breath itself, the floor holding you, light, water, someone who knows your name.
Somewhere along the way you'll lose count; when you do, stop, and just sit inside the part you can't number. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah there.

wordCard.voice: Ni'mah. A favor, a blessing, a grace. In 16:18, even one favor of God is too many to count. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a favor, a blessing, a grace; in 16:18, nimat Allah, God's favor.

carryVoice: Your line: uncountable. Even one favor opens into a thousand. That's day four hundred fifty-one.
